articles.title: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
articles.full_text:
Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)

However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”
articles.summary:
Meta has removed a controversial clause from its commercial terms of use after legal experts warned it could allow the company to scrape publisher websites and use the content to train its AI models. The reversal follows media scrutiny and a clarification from Meta that the provision never changed its web-crawling practices.

  • Core event: Meta's updated commercial terms stated the company could use any content from a business account's domains, web pages, or URLs to develop, improve, and train its products and services. Legal experts told Nieman Lab the language looked like a "remarkable provision" that could permit scraping of any publisher holding a Meta business account.
  • Background: A Meta spokesperson initially insisted the update did not reflect a change in how the company crawls the web, even as copyright litigation against AI developers—including Meta—continues. The company has since removed the clause entirely.
  • Impact: In a statement, Meta said it had "heard" the concerns and clarified that the consolidated crawling terms only applied to its ads and business products, adding that the change "does not change how Meta uses web crawlers." The episode highlights growing publisher sensitivity over AI training data and the scrutiny facing platform terms of service.
